extracted.intended_audience: regulated businesses, industry commenters, legal practitioners, policymakers, and participants in FTC rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether the FTC's Negative Option Rule and its rulemaking process complied with Section 18's procedural and substantive requirements (ANPR specificity, prevalence, specificity of prohibited acts, economic analysis, preemption, and related evidentiary showings). Useful for commenters, litigants, and advisers evaluating or challenging the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: ANPR specificity / description of area of inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 requires an ANPR to describe what the Commission aims to do so as to elicit public comment; an ANPR must invite interested parties to provide 'suggestions or alternative methods for achieving such objectives.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The whole purpose of section 18's requirement of a description of what the Commission aims to do is to elicit public comment to inform the Commission about its choices. Parties cannot possibly include alternative methods if the ANPR wholly fails to identify the objective (e.g., regulating misrepresentations in marketing of products with negative option features).

rubrics_metrics.name: ANPR focus on core negative-option Section 5 requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The ANPR tailored its inquiry by 'highlighting five basic section 5 requirements that negative option marketing must follow to avoid deception': (1) disclosure of material terms of a negative option offer; (2) clear and conspicuous disclosures; (3) pre-purchase disclosures; (4) consent; (5) cancellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ANPR did not contemplate broader regulation prohibiting all misrepresentations of material fact; the ANPR's topics define the reasonable scope for early notice and comment on negative option marketing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity requirement for rules under Section 18
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 requires the Commission to 'prescribe . . . rules which define with specificity acts or practices which are unfair or deceptive acts or practices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the prohibitions of section 5 are broad, trade regulation rules are needed to define with specificity conduct that violates the statute and to establish requirements to prevent unlawful conduct. A rule that prohibits any misrepresentation of material fact tied merely to the presence of a negative option feature fails this specificity requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence showing required to issue an NPRM
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 authorizes an NPRM 'only where it has reason to believe that the unfair or deceptive acts or practices which are the subject of the proposed rulemaking are prevalent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission may make a prevalence finding if (A) it has issued cease and desist orders regarding such acts or practices, or (B) any other information available to the Commission indicates a widespread pattern. High-level counts of cases or consumer complaints do not by themselves establish prevalence for an economy-wide rule; the evidence must show similarity and a widespread pattern relevant to the rule's actual scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary support for unfairness and deception theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Both unfairness and deception theories require sufficient evidence for a reviewing court to evaluate whether the Commission has met the legal predicate (particularly as it relates to reasonableness and materiality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unfairness explicitly requires a cost-benefit analysis relating to the practices at issue. Deception, while historically treated as always harmful, still requires evidence of materiality and reasonableness and an evidentiary basis that is similar to the contexts the rule will cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-benefit analysis for unfairness findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfairness explicitly requires a cost-benefit analysis relating to the practices at issue under Section 5(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission must analyze substantial injury, reasonable avoidability, and whether harms are outweighed by countervailing benefits to consumers or competition; failure to do so undermines an unfairness-based rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope to misrepresentations tied to negative-option conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule should not be economy-wide by prohibiting any misrepresentation of material fact simply because a product has a negative option feature; the Rule should focus on misrepresentations relating to deceptive terms of negative option features or other specific deceptive conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying the Rule to any material fact regardless of its relation to the negative option feature or regardless of consumer use overbroadly expands liability and fails Section 18's specificity requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require nexus to consumer experience/use of negative option feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule should not apply solely because a negative option feature exists; there should be a connection (e.g., consumer use or effect) tying the misrepresentation to the negative option feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Rule as criticized applies even if the consumer does not actually use the negative option feature; an appropriate rule should require a nexus so as not to sweep in unrelated misrepresentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using Section 18 to expand monetary remedies improperly
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule should not be a back-door effort to convert Section 5 broadly into a Section 18 rule in order to expand the Commission's ability to seek monetary relief contrary to AMG and other limits on equitable monetary remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because AMG limited the Commission's ability under Section 13(b) to obtain equitable monetary relief, the Commission must not circumvent legislative prerogative by using broad Section 18 rulemaking to obtain civil penalties across industries without appropriate statutory authority and guardrails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not shift tailoring burden to regulated entities via exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemptions provisions (allowing any person to petition for a partial or full exemption) do not cure overbreadth and should not serve as the Commission's primary method of tailoring a rule's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on post-promulgation petitions for exemptions shifts the burden (and cost) of tailoring the rule to regulated entities—especially burdensome for small businesses—and effectively delegates rule-shaping to petitioners rather than designing a narrowly tailored rule upfront.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust and representative economic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic estimates of the Rule's benefits and costs must be based on representative data and sound assumptions rather than small, self-selected samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deriving upper-bound benefits from complaints of 25 consumers in a single industry and extrapolating to the entire economy is not a representative sample and undermines confidence in benefit estimates; lack of frequency data (e.g., how often consumers have significant difficulty cancelling in-person) prevents proper weighting of estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how past enforcement cases support an economy-wide rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When generalizing from prior agency cases, the Commission must explain how the evidence in those limited cases is similar to the myriad contexts an economy-wide rule would apply to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely citing a set of past cases without connecting factual similarity to the broad range of industries and media covered by the Rule fails to meet specificity and prevalence requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity required when preempting state laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A Rule that preempts inconsistent State laws must specify the acts or practices the Commission deems deceptive with sufficient clarity to avoid placing in issue an indefinite variety of State laws and regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent specification of deceptive acts or practices, broad federal preemption can create confusion and jeopardize State laws and enforcement, harming consumers and regulated parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain appropriate procedural order and avoid premature sub-regulatory guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission should not disrupt a rulemaking by issuing sub-regulatory Enforcement Policy Statements or other guidance that alter the area of inquiry mid-process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuing an Enforcement Policy Statement regarding Negative Option Marketing while the rulemaking was ongoing changed the dynamic of the process; agencies should avoid using such guidance to pre-empt or expand the scope of notice-and-comment rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: ANPR must solicit sufficient early-stage public input for broader proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agency intends to pursue broader regulation later, the ANPR must be crafted to elicit meaningful early public comment (including alternative regulatory approaches) so stakeholders can inform the agency's choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ANPR that is too narrow (eliciting only 17 comments) cuts off valuable public comment on alternatives and undermines the legitimacy and lawfulness of any later expansion to a much broader NPRM.
